172 - The Hunger Games and Philosophy -: Suzanne Collins's Hunger Games trilogy, a bestselling dystopian series turned blockbuster films, follows Katniss Everdeen through an annual televised contest in which children fight to the death for the Capitol's entertainment. The premise invites serious questions: why do audiences enjoy watching suffering, does ordinary morality survive the arena, and can Katniss hold on to who she is while everyone, friend and tyrant alike, tries to turn her into a symbol? Chapters on Kant, moral luck, music, and interpretation show a story that is really about complicity, self-definition, and resistance.
173 - Inception and Philosophy - Because: Christopher Nolan's 2010 film Inception stars Leonardo DiCaprio as a thief who steals secrets from people's dreams and is hired, in a twist, to plant an idea instead. The film became famous for its nested dream levels and ambiguous spinning-top ending, which revive philosophy's oldest nightmare: how do you know you are not dreaming right now? The chapters probe Descartes and Plato's cave, free will, whether reality is what we choose to believe, and the ethics of manipulating another person's mind.
174 - Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why: Indiana Jones, the whip-cracking archaeologist Harrison Ford played from Raiders of the Lost Ark (1981) onward, is Hollywood's most beloved adventure hero, a professor who punches Nazis and races to put sacred relics in a museum. Behind the boulder chases lie real philosophical puzzles: does Indy actually matter to the plot, what makes artifacts worth preserving, and how should a man of facts respond to undeniable miracles? Chapters on Kant, Aristotle, virtue, feminism, and faith take the fedora seriously.
175 - Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing t: Iron Man is the Marvel Comics superhero Tony Stark, a billionaire weapons inventor whose high-tech suit has also headlined blockbuster films. Unlike gods or mutants, he is just a brilliant, flawed man, and that is the point: his stories ask whether great power brings great responsibility, what technology costs its maker and its users, and whether an alcoholic, womanizing engineer can ever atone for the deaths his products caused. Chapters on Heidegger, nanotech ethics, and Civil War guilt find tragedy beneath the armor.
178 - LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing: LEGO, the Danish construction toy of studded plastic bricks, has grown from children's playset into a creative medium spanning art installations, robotics kits, and The LEGO Movie. Its endless recombination makes it a natural philosophy kit: what is creativity if instructions and purist rules constrain it, when is one brick-built model the same object as another, and where does playful freedom end and rigid rule-worship begin? Chapters run the Ship of Theseus on a single set, defend architectural beauty, and take Emmet's double-decker couch seriously.
179 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy: The Legend of Zelda is Nintendo's landmark fantasy game series, running since 1986, in which the hero Link explores the land of Hyrule, solves dungeons, and rescues Princess Zelda. Because players guide Link rather than watch him, the games raise questions no film can: why do we weep for pixels, what happens to a hero who dies and resurrects endlessly, and does fast travel destroy the feel of a virtual place? Chapters range through Plato, existentialism, and the meaning of death in Hyrule.
180 - Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking: Mad Max is George Miller's Australian action franchise, from the 1979 original to Fury Road, set in a post-apocalyptic outback of raiders, road wars, and dwindling fuel. The Wasteland looks like chaos, but its warlords run functioning, if monstrous, regimes, which is exactly what makes it philosophically rich: is order possible without a state, what holds power in place when violence alone fails, and what ethics can be salvaged when civilization falls? Chapters put Hobbes, Marx, and anarchism on the dusty road.
181 - Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Thi: Lost, the ABC drama that ran from 2004 to 2010, stranded plane crash survivors on a mysterious island and became a television phenomenon for its flashbacks, time travel, and famously cryptic mythology. The island stories work because they isolate ordinary people and force philosophy's biggest questions: does my life matter, can the past be changed, is morality the same when no one is watching? Chapters take on time-travel metaphysics, ethical subjectivism, and the show's religious ending.
182 - Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing I: Mad Men, the acclaimed AMC series (2007-2015), follows Don Draper and his colleagues at a 1960s Madison Avenue advertising agency, an era of three-martini lunches, cigarette salesmanship, and casual sexism. Its appeal is moral vertigo: we root for a man selling cigarettes and concealing a stolen identity. The show becomes a philosophy seminar on the ethics of advertising, whether society's reasons reach women and outsiders, and whether people like Don can ever escape the past they refuse to remember.
183 - Metallica and Philosophy - A Crash: Metallica, formed in 1981, is the most influential band in heavy metal, known for punishing riffs and lyrics about death, addiction, madness, and rage. The songs are blunt, but they cut into real philosophical territory: does violent music corrupt character or refine it, why do we keep wanting what enslaves us, and what do bands owe their fans? Chapters on Kierkegaard, addiction, euthanasia, the Napster fight, and the song 'One' treat the band as a serious education in the dark side of life.
